planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this dwarf selection is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed to keep its compact, mat-forming habit true.

directions: This naturally compact sport of common winter savory forms a dense, low mat of narrow, glossy dark-green leaves rather than the upright woody shrublet of the species, making it well suited to edging paths, tumbling over container rims, and filling gaps between paving stones. The flavor is slightly milder and less resinous than standard winter savory but is used the same way, especially with beans, lentils, and slow-cooked meats. Shear lightly after the small white-to-lilac summer flowers fade to keep the mat tight and prevent bare, woody centers from developing. Because true dwarf plants must be propagated from cuttings or divisions to hold their compact form, start new plants vegetatively rather than from seed.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after all danger of frost has passed into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; propagate vegetatively, since seed-grown plants revert toward plain green foliage.

directions: Golden marjoram is a foliage sport of sweet marjoram selected for chartreuse-to-gold leaves that hold their brightest color in full sun and fade toward green in shade, while carrying the same mild, sweet, floral flavor as ordinary sweet marjoram. Its low, spreading habit and bright foliage make it as popular for edging and container plantings as it is for the kitchen, softening the look of an herb bed while remaining fully usable at the stove. Like the species it is frost-tender and grown as an annual outside zones 9-11, though potted plants can be overwintered indoors on a sunny windowsill. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep plants bushy and to delay the flower spikes that mark a drop in leaf flavor.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; propagate only by cuttings, as the cream-and-green leaf pattern does not come true from seed.

directions: This sport of sweet marjoram carries an irregular cream-to-white margin on each small oval leaf, giving mounded plants a frosted, two-tone look that reads more ornamental than the golden form while retaining the same delicate sweet-marjoram flavor in the green portion of the leaf. Some afternoon shade helps prevent the pale leaf margins from scorching in hot climates, unlike plain sweet marjoram, which tolerates full sun more readily. It is grown as a tender perennial in mild climates and as a container or annual herb elsewhere, and can be brought indoors over winter where space allows. Propagate only from stem cuttings, since seedlings do not reliably retain the variegated pattern.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in early spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil; divide established clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain the tight, variegated mat, since this cultivar is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: Little Angel is a naturally dwarf sport of great burnet, forming a tight, low mat of small pinnate leaves edged in cream-white rather than the tall, airy clumps of the straight species, with the same cool, cucumber-like flavor prized in salad burnet. Wiry stems carry small maroon button flowers well above the foliage from mid- to late summer, giving a second season of interest to what is otherwise grown as a low edging or container herb. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in early spring to maintain the tight habit and refresh vigor, since the variegation is a stable sport that holds true from division but not from seed. Harvest only the youngest inner leaves for eating, as older foliage toughens and the cucumber flavor fades.

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly at or just after the last frost once soil has warmed; this German-bred strain is grown exactly like ordinary summer savory but is selected for a bushier habit and higher essential-oil content.

directions: Aromata is a German (Erfurt-bred) seed strain of summer savory selected for a bushier, more branched habit and a notably higher essential-oil content in the leaf than common summer savory, giving a more concentrated peppery bite from the same amount of fresh or dried herb. It is grown exactly like ordinary summer savory, direct-sown after the last frost into full sun and lean, well-drained soil, then thinned and pinched to encourage branching. Because the oil content is higher, cooks can generally use it more sparingly than standard summer savory in the bean, lentil, and sausage dishes where the herb is traditional. Cut whole stems for drying just as the first flower buds appear, when oil concentration peaks.

planting.note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a cool site with some shade; germination is slow and often spread over the following spring.

directions: Alpine lovage is a true high-mountain relative of garden lovage native to the Alps, Pyrenees, and other European mountain ranges, forming a much smaller clump of finely divided, aromatic leaves that carry a milder, more herbaceous version of lovage's celery flavor. Unlike garden lovage, it thrives in cool, humus-rich, well-drained mountain soils and struggles in hot, humid lowland summers, making it best suited to alpine troughs, rock gardens, and cool-summer climates. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall so it experiences natural winter chilling, since seed loses viability quickly and often germinates unevenly the following spring. Young leaves can be used fresh as a celery-like potherb or dried for tea, and the whole plant has a long history of traditional culinary and medicinal use in Alpine farming communities.
